title: Teach me
hookLine: a warrior drops his bow, says "teach me," and falls silent: where the Gita's teaching begins
carry: the teaching begins when the student says "teach me"
tomorrow: your right is to the work. so do results matter at all?

cards: The conch shells have sounded. Arjuna, the finest archer on the field, asks Krishna, his friend and charioteer, to drive between the two armies so he can see who he's fighting. He sees teachers.
His bow slips from his hand. His mouth goes dry. He sits down in the chariot, and his eyes fill with tears.
Then he says something a warrior almost never says out loud.

teach.h: I AM YOUR STUDENT. TEACH ME.
teach.b: He turns to Krishna and says: my mind is confused about dharma. Tell me plainly what is better. shishyas te 'ham shadhi mam tvam prapannam: I am your student; teach me, I take refuge in you.
Then Sanjaya, the narrator, reports his last words before the teaching: na yotsya, I will not fight. And then a tiny word: iti. Thus.
Sanskrit has no quotation marks; iti does the job, closing someone's words.

teach.h: NA YOTSYA, ITI: HE FELL SILENT.
teach.b: After it, Sanjaya's voice: and having said that, he fell silent. Hold that silence.

Krishna, the text says, answers as if smiling, and the teaching of the Gita begins; most of its seven hundred verses are Krishna's. Notice the order. Krishna doesn't lecture a warrior who's sure of himself.
The teaching starts when Arjuna stops, admits he's lost, and asks. This is the oldest shape of Hindu learning: guru and shishya, teacher and student.
Later in the Gita, Krishna says it outright: learn by bowing, by asking questions, by serving, and those who have seen the truth will teach you.

That's why students touch a teacher's feet before a lesson, why many classes open with om saha navavatu, may it protect us both, teacher and student together, and why Guru Purnima is a day for thanking teachers.

teach.h: WHERE HIS VOICE STOPS, THE TEACHING STARTS.
teach.b: And iti marks the exact spot: where Arjuna's voice stops, the teaching starts. In this tradition, saying I don't know, teach me, isn't a weakness. It's the door.

how: Many Hindu students touch a teacher's feet or bow before a lesson and open study with the prayer om saha navavatu; Guru Purnima honors teachers each year. Readers of the Gita in Sanskrit learn early that iti closes quoted words.

o: why Hindu learning starts with asking a teacher

games.q: teacher and student — tap the pairs.

s: the Gita begins with Krishna lecturing a warrior who's sure of himself
it begins when Arjuna, lost, says: i am your student, teach me.
iti closes quoted words, like a quotation mark
na yotsya iti: "I will not fight," thus.
in the Gita, a student should never ask the teacher questions
4.34: learn by bowing, by asking, by serving.

games.q: a friend sees you touch your teacher's feet before class and asks if it's just old-fashioned. what do you say?
o: it says i'm ready to learn: the gita only begins when arjuna asks to be taught.
it's just manners, like saying hi.
it means the teacher is right about everything, no questions.
games.why: Arjuna said "i am your student, teach me" before Krishna taught a word. bowing, asking and serving is how the Gita says to learn (4.34).

practice: Bring to mind one person who taught you something real: a grandparent, a coach, a teacher.

If you pray, fold your hands and bow your head to them, the way students bow before a lesson; you might say om saha navavatu, may it protect us both. If you don't pray, just name silently what they taught you, and say thank you.

wordCard.voice: Two hundred core words. Today, iti, thus: the tiny word that closes Arjuna's na yotsya, and opens the space where the teaching begins. And shishya, student: what Arjuna calls himself.

orig.note: Sanskrit: I am your student; teach me, I take refuge in you (Bhagavad Gita 2.7).

carryVoice: The line for today: the teaching begins when the student says "teach me." Until tomorrow.
